report:
## What the evidence actually shows

The claim that abortion causes breast cancer is not supported by current scientific consensus. It originated from early case-control studies in the 1980s–90s that relied on women's self-reported abortion history, a method prone to "recall bias": women with breast cancer (searching for a cause) were more likely to disclose a past abortion than healthy women, artificially inflating apparent risk.

When researchers switched to prospective cohort designs—following women forward in time using medical records rather than self-report—the association disappeared. The landmark 1997 Danish study by Melbye et al., which tracked 1.5 million women, found no overall increased breast cancer risk from induced abortion (nytimes.com/1997/01/09/us/big-study-finds-no-link-in-abortion-and-cancer.html). This has been replicated in subsequent large cohort studies.

In 2003, the National Cancer Institute convened over 100 leading experts on pregnancy and breast cancer to review all existing evidence; they concluded induced abortion is not associated with an increase in breast cancer risk, a conclusion still maintained on NCI's site today (cancer.gov/types/breast/abortion-miscarriage-risk). The American Cancer Society reviewed the same evidence and reached the same conclusion, also noting a 2018 National Academies of Sciences report found no impact of abortion on breast cancer risk (cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html).

Major medical bodies—ACOG, WHO, NCI, ACS—now reject the hypothesis, while it continues to be promoted mainly by advocacy groups rather than peer-reviewed consensus (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abortion–breast_cancer_hypothesis).

**Conclusion:** The weight of higher-quality, methodologically rigorous evidence does not support a causal link between abortion and breast cancer. The belief persists largely due to flawed early studies and continued advocacy promotion, not current scientific consensus.
